title: One-Step Inequalities
standard_text: 6.9A write one-variable, one-step equations and inequalities to represent constraints or conditions within problems; 6.9B represent solutions for one-variable, one-step equations and inequalities on number lines; 6.10A model and solve one-variable, one-step equations and inequalities that represent problems, including geometric concepts; 6.10B determine if the given value(s) make(s) one-variable, one-step equations or inequalities true
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 inequality worksheets for Texas TEKS 6.9 and 6.10: read and write inequalities, solutions, number line graphs, solve one-step inequalities and word problems. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Open circle for < and >; closed circle for ≤ and ≥.
key_sub: x + 7 > 15, so x > 8. At least means ≥.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • An inequality compares two amounts with <, >, ≤ (at most) or ≥ (at least).
  • An inequality has many solutions: x > 4 means any number greater than 4.
  • On a number line, use an open circle for < and >, and a closed circle for ≤ and ≥. Shade toward the solutions.
  • Solve a one-step inequality like an equation: use the inverse operation on both sides.

Examples

Example

x + 7 > 15

Subtract 7 from both sides

Answer: x > 8

Example

4n ≤ 36

Divide both sides by 4

Answer: n ≤ 9

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Using an open circle for ≥ or ≤At least and at most include the number: closed circle.
Shading the wrong wayx > 8 means numbers to the right of 8.
Changing only one sideDo the same step to both sides.

faq.a: Represent solutions for one-variable, one-step equations and inequalities on number lines.
No. 8 is not greater than 8. It would be a solution of x ≥ 8.

faq.q: How is solving an inequality like solving an equation?
faq.a: You use inverse operations on both sides. In Grade 6 the numbers are positive, so the sign stays the same.

items.q: What does n > 5 mean?
c: n is greater than or equal to 5
n is less than or equal to 5
items.e: Read from left to right: n is greater than 5. The symbol opens toward n, the greater side.

items.q: What does z < 38 mean?
c: z is less than or equal to 38
z is greater than or equal to 38
items.e: Read from left to right: z is less than 38. The point of the symbol is toward z, the lesser side.

items.q: What does x ≥ 18 mean?
c: x is less than or equal to 18
x is greater than or equal to 18
items.e: Read from left to right: x is greater than or equal to 18. The line under the symbol means “or equal to,” so x can also be 18.

items.q: What does r ≤ 14 mean?
c: r is less than or equal to 14
r is greater than or equal to 14
items.e: Read from left to right: r is less than or equal to 14. The line under the symbol means “or equal to,” so r can also be 14.

items.q: What does y > 12 mean?
c: y is less than or equal to 12
y is greater than or equal to 12
items.e: Read from left to right: y is greater than 12. The symbol opens toward y, the greater side.

items.q: What does p < 36 mean?
c: p is less than or equal to 36
p is greater than or equal to 36
items.e: Read from left to right: p is less than 36. The point of the symbol is toward p, the lesser side.

items.q: Which inequality means “m is less than 8”?
items.e: “m is less than 8” is written m < 8, with m first. 8 < m says “8 is less than m,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which inequality means “t is greater than 21”?
items.e: “t is greater than 21” is written t > 21, with t first. 21 > t says “21 is greater than t,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which inequality means “k is less than or equal to 35”?
items.e: “k is less than or equal to 35” is written k ≤ 35, with k first. 35 ≤ k says “35 is less than or equal to k,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which inequality means “w is greater than or equal to 15”?
items.e: “w is greater than or equal to 15” is written w ≥ 15, with w first. 15 ≥ w says “15 is greater than or equal to w,” which is the opposite.

items.q: Which inequality shows “y is more than 6”?
items.e: “More than 6” does not include 6, so use >. The inequality is y > 6.

items.q: Which inequality shows “w is greater than 19”?
items.e: “Greater than 19” does not include 19, so use >. The inequality is w > 19.

items.q: Which inequality shows “m is over 15”?
items.e: “Over 15” does not include 15, so use >. The inequality is m > 15.

items.q: Which inequality shows “t is less than 22”?
items.e: “Less than 22” does not include 22, so use <. The inequality is t < 22.

items.q: Which inequality shows “x is under 46”?
items.e: “Under 46” does not include 46, so use <. The inequality is x < 46.

items.q: Which inequality shows “r is below 23”?
items.e: “Below 23” does not include 23, so use <. The inequality is r < 23.

items.q: Which inequality shows “k is at least 42”?
items.e: “At least 42” means 42 or more, so use ≥. The inequality is k ≥ 42.

items.q: Which inequality shows “n is no less than 3”?
items.e: “No less than 3” means 3 or more, so use ≥. The inequality is n ≥ 3.

items.q: Which inequality shows “z is at most 43”?
items.e: “At most 43” means 43 or less, so use ≤. The inequality is z ≤ 43.

items.q: Which inequality shows “p is no more than 47”?
items.e: “No more than 47” means 47 or less, so use ≤. The inequality is p ≤ 47.

items.q: Which number is a solution of x > 9?
items.e: Test each number in x > 9: 9 12 > 9 is true; 9 > 9 is false; 8 > 9 is false; 3 > 9 is false. Only 9 12 makes it true. 9 is not a solution, because 9 is not greater than itself.

items.q: Which number is a solution of p < 7?
items.e: Test each number in p < 7: 6.9 < 7 is true; 7 < 7 is false; 7.1 < 7 is false; 8 < 7 is false. Only 6.9 makes it true. 7 is not a solution, because 7 is not less than itself.

items.q: Which number is a solution of z ≥ 12?
items.e: Test each number in z ≥ 12: 12 ≥ 12 is true; 11 ≥ 12 is false; 11 12 ≥ 12 is false; 2 ≥ 12 is false. Only 12 makes it true. ≥ and ≤ include the number itself.

items.q: Which number is a solution of r ≤ 15?
items.e: Test each number in r ≤ 15: 15 ≤ 15 is true; 16 ≤ 15 is false; 15 12 ≤ 15 is false; 20 ≤ 15 is false. Only 15 makes it true. ≥ and ≤ include the number itself.

items.q: Which number is a solution of y > −2?
items.e: Test each number in y > −2: 0 > −2 is true; −2 > −2 is false; −5 > −2 is false; −3 > −2 is false. Only 0 makes it true. −2 is not a solution, because −2 is not greater than itself. On a number line, −5 is to the left of −2, so −5 < −2.

items.q: Which number is a solution of t < −4?
items.e: Test each number in t < −4: −6 < −4 is true; −4 < −4 is false; −2 < −4 is false; 0 < −4 is false. Only −6 makes it true. −4 is not a solution, because −4 is not less than itself. On a number line, −6 is to the left of −4, so −6 < −4.

items.q: Which number is a solution of n > 2 12?
items.e: Test each number in n > 2 12: 3 > 2 12 is true; 2 12 > 2 12 is false; 2 > 2 12 is false; 1 12 > 2 12 is false. Only 3 makes it true. 2 12 is not a solution, because 2 12 is not greater than itself.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of m > 5?
items.e: Test each number in m > 5: 5 > 5 is false; 5.1 > 5 is true; 6 > 5 is true; 20 > 5 is true. 5 is the only one that makes it false. The number itself is not a solution of m > 5.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of k < 10?
items.e: Test each number in k < 10: 10 < 10 is false; 9.9 < 10 is true; 9 < 10 is true; 0 < 10 is true. 10 is the only one that makes it false. The number itself is not a solution of k < 10.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of w ≥ 8?
items.e: Test each number in w ≥ 8: 7 12 ≥ 8 is false; 8 ≥ 8 is true; 8 12 ≥ 8 is true; 30 ≥ 8 is true. 7 12 is the only one that makes it false.

items.q: Which number is not a solution of r ≤ −3?
items.e: Test each number in r ≤ −3: −2 ≤ −3 is false; −3 ≤ −3 is true; −4 ≤ −3 is true; −10 ≤ −3 is true. −2 is the only one that makes it false.

items.q: Is 7 a solution of r > 7?
c: No, because only numbers less than 7 are solutions
No, because 7 is not greater than 7
Yes, because 7 is the number in the inequality
items.e: 7 > 7 is false. The sign has no “or equal to,” so 7 is left out.

items.q: Is 11 a solution of y ≤ 11?
c: Yes, because every number is a solution
No, the circle at 11 is open
No, because 11 is not less than 11
items.e: 11 ≤ 11 is true. The line under the sign means “or equal to,” so 11 is included.

items.q: Is 4 a solution of t < 4?
c: Yes, because 4 is the number in the inequality
No, because only numbers greater than 4 are solutions
No, because 4 is not less than 4
items.e: 4 < 4 is false. The sign has no “or equal to,” so 4 is left out.

items.q: Is 20 a solution of n ≥ 20?
c: No, because 20 is not greater than 20
Yes, because every number is a solution
No, the circle at 20 is open
items.e: 20 ≥ 20 is true. The line under the sign means “or equal to,” so 20 is included.

items.q: Which list has only solutions of n ≤ 4?
items.e: Every number in 1, 3, 4 makes n ≤ 4 true. Each other list has a number that does not work: 5 in 1, 3, 5; 6 in 4, 6, 8; 9 in 0, 2, 9.

items.q: Which list has only solutions of m > 6?
items.e: Every number in 6.5, 7, 10 makes m > 6 true. Each other list has a number that does not work: 6 in 6, 7, 10; 2 in 2, 4, 8; 5 in 5, 6.5, 9.

items.q: Which list has only solutions of k < 0?
items.e: Every number in −1, −0.5, −8 makes k < 0 true. Each other list has a number that does not work: 0 in −1, 0, −3; 2 in −4, −2, 2; 0.5 in −5, −1, 0.5.

items.q: How many solutions does x > 3 have?
items.e: Every number greater than 3 works: 4, 3.5, 3.01, 100, 1,000,000 and so on. There is no end, so there are infinitely many solutions.

items.q: How many solutions does y < 10 have?
items.e: Not just whole numbers work. 9.5, 2.25, 0 and −40 are also less than 10. There is no end, so there are infinitely many solutions.

items.e: The circle is at 4. The circle is open, so 4 is not included, and the arrow points right (greater numbers), so the inequality is x > 4.

items.q: Which inequality does the graph show?

items.q: Which describes the graph of x ≤ 3 on a number line?
c: Closed circle at 3, shaded to the right
Open circle at 3, shaded to the left
Closed circle at 3, shaded to the left
Open circle at 3, shaded to the right
items.e: x ≤ 3 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 3 itself is a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers.

items.q: Which describes the graph of x > 8 on a number line?
c: Open circle at 8, shaded to the right
Closed circle at 8, shaded to the left
Closed circle at 8, shaded to the right
Open circle at 8, shaded to the left
items.e: x > 8 has an open circle, because 8 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers.

items.q: Which describes the graph of x < −1 on a number line?
c: Open circle at −1, shaded to the right
Closed circle at −1, shaded to the right
Open circle at −1, shaded to the left
Closed circle at −1, shaded to the left
items.e: x < −1 has an open circle, because −1 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers.

items.q: Which describes the graph of x ≥ 25 on a number line?
c: Open circle at 25, shaded to the left
Open circle at 25, shaded to the right
Closed circle at 25, shaded to the left
Closed circle at 25, shaded to the right
items.e: x ≥ 25 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 25 itself is a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers.

items.q: Grace graphed x ≥ 2 like this. What is wrong?
c: The arrow should point the other way
The circle should be closed (filled in)
items.e: x ≥ 2 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 2 itself is a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers. Grace’s graph shows x > 2 instead.

items.q: Zoe graphed x < 6 like this. What is wrong?
c: The arrow should point to the left
The circle should be closed (filled in)
items.e: x < 6 has an open circle, because 6 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers. Zoe’s graph shows x > 6 instead.

items.q: Lucia graphed x ≤ −4 like this. What is wrong?
c: The circle should be closed (filled in)
The arrow should point the other way
items.e: x ≤ −4 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because −4 itself is a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers. Lucia’s graph shows x < −4 instead.

items.q: Carlos graphed x > 10 like this. What is wrong?
c: The circle should be closed (filled in)
The arrow should point to the right
items.e: x > 10 has an open circle, because 10 itself is not a solution, and the arrow points right, toward greater numbers. Carlos’s graph shows x < 10 instead.

items.q: Which number is a solution shown by the graph?
items.e: The graph shows x < 5. Test each number in x < 5: 2 < 5 is true; 5 < 5 is false; 6 < 5 is false; 9 < 5 is false. The open circle means 5 is not included.

items.q: Which number is a solution shown by the graph?
items.e: The graph shows x ≥ −1. Test each number in x ≥ −1: −1 ≥ −1 is true; −2 ≥ −1 is false; −4 ≥ −1 is false; −1.5 ≥ −1 is false. The closed circle means −1 is included.

items.q: To ride a roller coaster, you must be at least 48 inches tall. Let h be a rider’s height in inches. Which inequality shows the heights that can ride?
items.e: “At least 48” means 48 inches or taller. A rider who is exactly 48 inches can ride, so use ≥: h ≥ 48.

items.q: A water slide says: “Riders must be at least 54 inches tall.” Four friends measured their heights. Which height is allowed on the slide?
items.e: The heights allowed are h ≥ 54. 54 is equal to 54, and ≥ includes equal, so it is allowed. The others are less than 54.

items.q: At a restaurant, kids under 12 eat free. Let a be a child’s age in years. Which inequality shows the ages that eat free?
items.e: “Under 12” means less than 12. A child who is 12 does not eat free, so use <, not ≤: a < 12.

items.q: Mateo has $25 to spend on a gift. Let c be the cost of the gift in dollars. Which inequality shows the costs he can pay?
items.e: Mateo can spend all $25 or less, so the cost is at most 25: c ≤ 25.

items.q: The speed limit on a road is 55 miles per hour. The legal speeds are s ≤ 55. Which speed is not allowed?
items.e: 57 > 55, so 57 mph is over the limit. 55 mph is exactly the limit, and ≤ includes it.

items.q: A sign in an elevator says: “No more than 15 people.” Let p be the number of people. Which numbers make sense as solutions?
c: Every number less than or equal to 15
items.e: p ≤ 15, but you cannot have 3.5 or −2 people. Only whole numbers make sense, and 15 is allowed, so the solutions are 0, 1, 2, … , 15.

items.q: A class has fewer than 25 students. What is the greatest number of students the class could have?
items.e: “Fewer than 25” means s < 25, so 25 is not allowed. Students come in whole numbers, so the greatest is 24. (24.5 students makes no sense.)

items.q: To win a prize, you need a score of more than 90 points. Scores are whole numbers. What is the least score that wins?
items.e: “More than 90” means s > 90, so 90 does not win. The next whole number is 91. (100 also wins, but it is not the least.)

items.q: Water freezes when the temperature is below 32°F. Let t be the temperature in °F. How many temperatures are solutions of t < 32?
c: Only the whole numbers from 0 to 31
items.e: Any temperature less than 32 works: 31.9, 20, 0, −5 and so on. Temperatures do not have to be whole numbers, and there is no end, so there are infinitely many solutions.

items.q: An airline says a checked bag can weigh at most 40 pounds. Which bag weight is allowed?
items.e: “At most 40” means w ≤ 40. 40 = 40, so a 40-pound bag is allowed. The others are more than 40.

items.q: Which rule could this graph show? (x is age in years.)
c: You must be at least 12 years old
You can be at most 12 years old
You must be over 12 years old
You must be under 12 years old
items.e: The closed circle at 12 means 12 is included, and the arrow points right. That is x ≥ 12: 12 or older, which is “at least 12.” “Over 12” would need an open circle.

items.q: Which sentence could this graph show? (x is the temperature in °F.)
items.e: The open circle at 5 means 5 is not included, and the arrow points left. That is x < 5, “below 5.” “At most 5” would need a closed circle.

items.q: A field trip will happen only if at least 20 students sign up. Let s be the number of students who sign up. Which inequality shows when the trip will happen?
items.e: “At least 20” means 20 or more. A common mistake is to use ≤ or < because of the word “least.” The answer is s ≥ 20.

items.q: A phone plan lets you use no more than 10 GB of data each month. Let d be the data used in GB. Which inequality matches the plan?
items.e: “No more than 10” means 10 or less, and 10 is allowed: d ≤ 10.

items.q: Emma’s plant is taller than 14 centimeters. Which could be the height of the plant?
items.e: “Taller than 14” means h > 14. Only 14.5 is greater than 14. A plant that is exactly 14 cm is not taller than 14 cm.

items.q: A recipe says to bake the bread for at least 30 minutes. Let t be the baking time in minutes. Which inequality shows the baking times?
items.e: “At least 30 minutes” means 30 minutes or longer: t ≥ 30.

items.q: An elevator can carry a maximum of 3,000 pounds. Let w be the weight it carries in pounds. Which inequality shows the weights it can carry?
items.e: The maximum is the greatest weight allowed, and 3,000 pounds itself is allowed: w ≤ 3,000.

items.q: A soccer league needs a minimum of 11 players on each team. Ava writes p ≤ 11. Which is right?
c: p < 11, because the team must be smaller
p ≥ 11, because a minimum of 11 means 11 or more
p > 11, because the minimum is not included
p ≤ 11 is right, because a minimum is a small number
items.e: A minimum is the least number allowed. A team can have 11 players or more, so p ≥ 11.

items.q: Liam says x > 3 has only 4 solutions: 4, 5, 6 and 7. Is he right?
c: No. Every number greater than 3 works, so there are infinitely many
Yes. Those are all the solutions
items.e: 8, 3.5, 100 and 1,000 are also greater than 3. The solutions never end, so x > 3 has infinitely many solutions. 3 is not one of them.

items.q: In a school zone, cars must drive no faster than 15 mph. Which describes the graph of the speeds s ≤ 15?
c: Open circle at 15, shaded to the right
Open circle at 15, shaded to the left
Closed circle at 15, shaded to the right
Closed circle at 15, shaded to the left
items.e: s ≤ 15 has a closed (filled-in) circle, because 15 itself is a solution, and the arrow points left, toward lesser numbers.
